hints: Compare the two functional groups in V, the $\text{-COOH}$ group and the $\text{C=C}$ bond, and recall which one is reduced by $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ in dry ether.
walkthrough:
Spot the two possible reaction sites in V**
Look at Fig. 4.1. On the left you have a carboxylic acid group, $\text{-COOH}$, and on the right you have an alkene, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{=CH-}$. You are adding a very strong reducing agent, $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ in excess, so ask which site it attacks.

Reduce the acid, leave the alkene alone**
$\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ reduces carboxylic acids all the way to primary alcohols: $\text{R-COOH}$ becomes $\text{R-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. It does not reduce an isolated $\text{C=C}$ bond under these conditions. So the $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH=CH}_{2}$ tail stays exactly as it is, and only the $\text{HO-C=O}$ head becomes $\text{HO-CH}_{2}\text{-}$. That gives $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH=CH}_{2}$.
Final answer: W is $\text{HO-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH=CH}_{2}$ (but-3-en-1-ol). The $\text{-COOH}$ is reduced to $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, the $\text{C=C}$ is unchanged.

hints: Think about what happens to the oxidation level of the carboxyl carbon when $\text{-COOH}$ becomes $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, whether oxygen is lost or hydrogen is gained.
walkthrough:
Link oxygen loss to reduction**
In V to W the carbon of the acid group loses bonded oxygen and gains hydrogen to form $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. Gain of hydrogen and loss of oxygen is reduction, so the $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ that supplies hydride, $\text{H}^{-}$, is acting as a reducing agent.

hints: Look at Fig. 4.2 and focus only on what changes: the $\text{C=C}$ becomes $\text{-CH(OH)-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ while the $\text{-COOH}$ group is untouched.
walkthrough:
Recognise dihydroxylation, not cleavage**
In Z the double bond has gained two $\text{-OH}$ groups, one on each carbon, to give a diol. The carbon skeleton is still intact and the acid group is unchanged. That is mild oxidation of an alkene, not hot concentrated oxidative cleavage.

Choose the mild oxidising conditions**
The classic AS reagent for alkene to diol is cold and dilute acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}$. Hot concentrated $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ would break the $\text{C=C}$ completely, which has not happened here, so you must state cold and dilute.

hints: Count all C, H and O atoms in the displayed structure of Z in Fig. 4.2 to get the molecular formula first, then simplify.
walkthrough:
Count then simplify**
Count from Z, $\text{HOOC-CH}_{2}\text{-CH(OH)-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$: there are 4 carbons, 8 hydrogens and 4 oxygens, so molecular formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{4}$. Divide the subscripts by their highest common factor, 4, to get the simplest ratio $\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}$, which is the empirical formula.

hints: Recall the quick rule: a carbon with a double bond ($\text{C=C}$ or $\text{C=O}$) is $\text{sp}^{2}$, a carbon with four single sigma bonds is $\text{sp}^{3}$.
Label each of the four carbons in V in Fig. 4.1 as double bonded or single bonded only, then total each type.
walkthrough:
Pick out the sp2 carbons**
Any carbon involved in a double bond is $\text{sp}^{2}$ with trigonal planar geometry. In V, $\text{HO-C(=O)-CH}_{2}\text{-CH=CH}_{2}$, the carboxyl carbon ($\text{C=O}$) counts as one, plus the two alkene carbons ($\text{C=C}$) makes three in total.

Pick out the sp3 carbons**
Any carbon with four single bonds is $\text{sp}^{3}$ with tetrahedral geometry. Only the $\text{CH}_{2}$ group between the $\text{COOH}$ and the $\text{C=C}$ fits this, so there is just 1 $\text{sp}^{3}$ carbon. Check: 3 + 1 = 4 carbons, which matches V.
Final answer: $\text{sp}^{2}$: 3 carbon atoms; $\text{sp}^{3}$: 1 carbon atom.

hints: Use the two effervescence tests to decide the functional group: no $\text{CO}_{2}$ with $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$ but $\text{H}_{2}$ with Na points to an alcohol, not a carboxylic acid.

Combine the yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}$(aq) with the $M_{r}$ of 88 and an unbranched saturated mono-alcohol formula $\text{C}_{n}\text{H}_{2n+2}\text{O}$ to find n and the position of the $\text{-OH}$.
walkthrough:
Narrow to a straight chain alcohol**
No fizz with $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$ rules out a carboxylic acid. Fizz with sodium shows an $\text{-OH}$ group, so Q is an alcohol. It has only C, H and O, is saturated, has one functional group and no branching, so it must be a straight chain $\text{C}_{n}\text{H}_{2n+2}\text{O}$ alcohol.

Use Mr to find the chain length**
Let the formula be $\text{C}_{n}\text{H}_{2n+2}\text{O}$. Then $M_{r} = 12n + (2n+2) + 16 = 14n + 18 = 88$. Solving gives $14n = 70$, so $n = 5$. Q is a $\text{C}_{5}$ alcohol, $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$.

Place the OH using the iodoform test**
A yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}$(aq) is the triiodomethane test for $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)-}$. On a straight 5 carbon chain this can only be pentan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. Pentan-3-ol would not give the test and pentan-1-ol has $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, not $\text{-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)OH}$.

Final answer: Q is pentan-2-ol: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-CH(OH)-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{3}$ (skeletal structure showing a straight 5C chain with OH on C2, containing $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)-}$).
